prompt: A colleague says a serverless function "runs without servers". What is actually the case?
hint: The word describes who manages the machines.

choices.text: It runs on the provider's servers, which you never see or manage
choices.why: Right. The servers exist; choosing, patching and counting them is the provider's job.

choices.text: It runs in the visitor's browser, so no server is involved
choices.why: That is front-end code. A function runs on the provider's machines, in a region or at the edge.

choices.text: It runs on one server the provider reserves for your account
choices.why: Nothing is reserved: copies are created as requests arrive and live on whatever machines the provider picks.

choices.text: It runs on a machine you rent, patched by the provider
choices.why: That is closer to a managed virtual machine. With a function you rent no machine at all; you pay per call.

prompt: An autoscaling group of virtual machines and a Lambda function both follow traffic. What does the function do that the group, as lesson 4 set it up, does not?
hint: Think about a quiet night.

choices.text: Add capacity as traffic rises
choices.why: Both do that; growing with traffic is what autoscaling is for.

choices.text: Run programs written in Python
choices.why: A virtual machine runs any language installed on it, so this is not the difference.

choices.text: Scale down to zero copies
choices.why: Right. The group keeps a minimum running for the first request; a function has no minimum, and the first request creates a copy.

choices.text: Answer HTTP requests behind a load balancer
choices.why: The group does that too; lesson 6 puts a load balancer in front of exactly such a group.

prompt: A team moves its API from PaaS to functions and announces "no more operations work". A library the functions import gets a published vulnerability. Who updates it?
hint: Which side of lesson 1's line is the code on?

choices.text: The provider, because it now runs the runtime
choices.why: The provider updates the runtime and the operating system, not the libraries inside your package.

choices.text: Nobody: each copy lives briefly, so the flaw is never exploitable
choices.why: A request is all an exploit needs, and a short-lived copy still handles it with the vulnerable code.

choices.text: The provider, provided the team pays for a support plan
choices.why: A support plan buys help, not ownership: what is inside your package stays yours either way.

choices.text: The team: the code and its imports stay on its side
choices.why: Right. The provider runs the runtime and the machines; the package you upload, libraries included, is yours.

prompt: On Lambda, the one size you still choose for a function is its ___, and the share of processor follows it in proportion.
hint: It is measured in MB.

prompt: In a Lambda handler file, where does code run once per execution environment rather than on every call?
hint: Look at what sits above `def handler`.

choices.text: Inside the handler, before its return
choices.why: Everything inside the handler runs on every call.

choices.text: At module level, outside the handler
choices.why: Right. The file is loaded once when the environment starts; only the handler runs per call.

choices.text: In the `context` object
choices.why: `context` is data about the call that the platform passes in, not code you write.

choices.text: In a helper function the handler calls
choices.why: A helper called from the handler runs whenever the handler does, so on every call.

prompt: Behind an API gateway, a handler returns `{"statusCode": 200, "body": {"message": "hi"}}`. What is wrong with it?
hint: Look at the type of each value.

choices.text: The status code has to be the string "200"
choices.why: It is a number in this format, as in the lesson's handler.

choices.text: Every response must carry a `headers` key
choices.why: Headers are optional; the lesson's handler sets one only to say the body is JSON.

choices.text: A handler prints its response instead of returning it
choices.why: Printing writes to the function's log; the gateway reads the return value.

choices.text: The body has to be a string
choices.why: Right. The gateway copies the body into the HTTP response as text; the lesson's handler passes its dict through `json.dumps` for that reason.

prompt: A handler increments a module-level counter and returns it. Two requests from the same person, a second apart, both get 1. What happened?
hint: Each copy has its own module.

choices.text: Two different execution environments served them
choices.why: Right. Each environment has its own counter, and nothing sends one person to the same copy twice.

choices.text: The counter is reset at the start of every call
choices.why: Module-level code runs once per environment, not per call; in one warm environment the counter keeps growing.

choices.text: The second request was a retry of the first one
choices.why: A retry is a new call; in the same environment it would still have read 2.

choices.text: Python cannot change a module variable from inside a function
choices.why: With `global` it can, and that is what the lesson's handler does.

prompt: A call still running when its configured ___ runs out is stopped by the platform, and the caller sees a failure.
hint: On Lambda it defaults to 3 seconds.

prompt: Calling the handler as a Python function on a laptop, with a hand-written event, tests what?
hint: Lambda is not involved.

choices.text: How long a cold start takes once it runs on Lambda
choices.why: A cold start only exists on the platform; the laptop has no execution environment to create.

choices.text: Whether the IAM role grants the function enough permission
choices.why: Permissions are checked by the provider when the function calls a service, which never happens here.

choices.text: The contract: what goes in and what comes out
choices.why: Right. It checks the logic against the event you wrote, and nothing about the platform.

choices.text: Whether the gateway is set up to send requests to this handler
choices.why: The gateway's configuration lives on the platform; the local call skips the gateway entirely.

prompt: On the laptop, the second call printed `"served_by_this_copy": 2`. What does that tell you about Lambda?
hint: How many Python processes ran the two calls?

choices.text: That Lambda keeps state between calls, so the counter is safe to use
choices.why: Lambda keeps nothing it promises; the laptop's single process is not how the platform behaves.

choices.text: Nothing, since both calls shared one process
choices.why: Right, and Lambda does not promise that. The laptop shows the most optimistic case, one copy serving everything.

choices.text: That Lambda would answer 2 as well, since the code is identical
choices.why: Identical code in a different environment starts its own counter at 1.

choices.text: That the second call was a cold start
choices.why: A cold start loads the module afresh, and the counter would have read 1.

prompt: A handler reads `event["queryStringParameters"]["name"]`. Its local tests always pass an event with a query string, and all pass. In production some requests fail. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Which case did the lesson's second local call test?

choices.text: The platform strips query strings before calling the handler
choices.why: Then every request would fail, not some of them.

choices.text: Production runs a Python version that reads dicts differently
choices.why: Dictionary lookups behave the same across Python 3 versions; the event is what differs.

choices.text: The gateway sends the query string unparsed, as one string
choices.why: For this integration it arrives parsed into a dict; if it did not, no request would work.

choices.text: Some events come without that key, or with null in it
choices.why: Right: requests with no query string. The tests never wrote that event, so they could not find it; `.get` with `or {}` handles it.

prompt: Match each trigger to what the event it hands the function carries.
hint: The event says what happened, not always the data itself.

pairs.left: An HTTP request through a gateway
pairs.right: A path, headers and a query string

pairs.left: A file landing in a bucket
pairs.right: The bucket's name and the object's key
A notice that the rule fired, and when

right_distractors: The contents of the uploaded file

prompt: A function that sends a welcome e-mail reads messages from an SQS standard queue. Some people get the e-mail twice, though the function never failed. What fixes it?
hint: Delivery is at least once.

choices.text: Record each message's id and skip ids already handled
choices.why: Right. A duplicate is part of the contract, so the handler has to be idempotent.

choices.text: Raise the timeout so that no call is ever cut off
choices.why: No call failed; duplicates arrive even when every call succeeds.

choices.text: Give the function more memory so each call ends sooner
choices.why: Speed does not change delivery; the same message is still delivered twice.

choices.text: Replace the queue with a schedule that runs hourly
choices.why: It trades the duplicates for an hour of delay and still does not make the handler safe to run twice.

prompt: Which of these calls have nobody waiting for the function's return value? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only one kind of trigger has a caller at the other end.

choices.text: A photo landing in a bucket
choices.why: Right. The result is the thumbnail it writes, and nobody is waiting on the call.

choices.text: A browser calling a function URL
choices.why: A browser waits for the response, and the return value becomes it.

choices.text: A rule that fires every night
choices.why: Right. A schedule has no caller; the result is whatever the function changed.

choices.text: A batch taken off a queue
choices.why: Right. Whoever put the messages there has moved on; a failure goes back on the queue rather than to a person.

prompt: A function triggered by files in a bucket has failed on every event for a week, and nobody noticed. What would have made the failure visible?
hint: There is no user to complain.

choices.text: A longer timeout, so every event has time to finish
choices.why: Nothing says the events timed out, and a longer timeout reports nothing to anybody.

choices.text: An HTTP trigger in front of the bucket
choices.why: It adds a caller, but the uploads still arrive as bucket events that nobody watches.

choices.text: A dead-letter queue with an alarm on it
choices.why: Right. Failed events are kept aside, and the alarm tells a person they are piling up.

choices.text: More memory, so that the function stops failing
choices.why: It guesses at a cause nobody has seen, and a failure of any other kind stays just as silent.

prompt: Put the phases of a cold start on Lambda in order.
hint: Your code cannot run before there is somewhere to run it.
items: A request arrives and no execution environment is free
The platform creates an environment and puts your code in it
The runtime starts and runs your module-level code
The handler is called with the event
The environment is frozen and kept for the next request
trap: Module-level code before the environment is the usual slip: the init runs inside an environment that already exists.

prompt: Why is the first request after a quiet hour slower than the ones right after it?
hint: What had to exist before the handler could run?

choices.text: The provider slows down functions that are rarely called
choices.why: Nothing in the platform penalises a quiet function; it simply has no copy ready.

choices.text: No warm copy was left, so one had to be built
choices.why: Right. A new environment was created and initialised first: the cold start. The requests after it reuse it.

choices.text: The function's code is compiled again every hour
choices.why: Nothing is recompiled on a timer; the delay comes from creating an environment.

choices.text: The API gateway's cache had been emptied
choices.why: A gateway cache is not the cause; the delay is in the function starting.

prompt: A handler creates its database client inside the handler. What changes when that line moves to module level?
hint: Module level runs once per environment.

choices.text: Cold starts become shorter
choices.why: If anything they grow: the client is now created during the init, while the warm calls get cheaper.

choices.text: Every environment of the function shares one client
choices.why: Each environment has its own module, so each builds its own client.

choices.text: Warm calls reuse the client
choices.why: Right. It is paid once per environment and reused by every warm call after that.

choices.text: Nothing, because Lambda runs the whole file on each call
choices.why: Only the handler runs per call; the file is loaded once per environment.

prompt: Once an hour, 50 requests reach a function in the same second, and no warm environment is left from the hour before. What do they meet?
hint: One environment serves one request at a time.

choices.text: Only the first pays; the other 49 queue for its environment
choices.why: An environment serves one request at a time, and the platform creates more rather than queue 49 behind it.

choices.text: None, because Lambda always keeps one environment warm
choices.why: Without provisioned concurrency nothing is kept warm on purpose; a quiet hour can leave none.

choices.text: All 50 are refused until one environment is ready
choices.why: The platform creates environments for them; it does not refuse the burst.

choices.text: A cold start each, since every one needs a new environment
choices.why: Right. A burst is where cold starts cluster: fifty requests, fifty environments created at once.

prompt: On Lambda, keeping a number of environments initialised in advance, charged for whether they are used or not, is called provisioned ___.
hint: How many copies run at once.

prompt: A function configured with 1,024 MB runs for 250 ms. How many GB-seconds does one call use?
hint: Memory in GB times duration in seconds.

prompt: A function answers 2 million calls a month at 256 MB and 200 ms each. How many GB-seconds is that in the month?
hint: 256 MB is a quarter of a GB.

prompt: With the sheet's x86 prices and no free tier, what do 10 million requests at 512 MB and 120 ms cost in a month, in USD?
hint: Two meters: requests, then GB-seconds.

prompt: The lesson's API doubles its traffic to 6 million requests a month, still at 512 MB and 120 ms. With the free tier subtracted, what does the month cost, in USD?
hint: Check the GB-seconds against the 400,000 allowance before pricing them.

prompt: A function spends 100 ms of its 120 ms waiting for a database to answer. How is the waiting billed on Lambda?
hint: What does a GB-second measure?

choices.text: Like work: GB-seconds count the held time
choices.why: Right. The meter runs from the call's start to its return, busy or waiting.

choices.text: Not at all: Lambda bills processor time alone
choices.why: That is the choice Cloudflare makes for Workers; Lambda's GB-seconds count the whole duration.

choices.text: At the Arm rate, which is lower
choices.why: The rate depends on the architecture you chose, not on what the code is doing.

choices.text: As extra requests, one for every database query
choices.why: The request meter counts calls to the function, not what the function calls.

prompt: The sheet gives an m7g.large in us-east-1, on demand, at 0.08160 USD an hour. With a 730-hour month and the function at 1.20 USD per million requests, where is the crossover, in millions of requests a month?
hint: The machine's month divided by the function's price per million.

prompt: Why does the lesson also compare the function with two t3.medium and a load balancer, and not only with one machine?
hint: What does a function give you that one machine does not?

choices.text: Because the function needs a load balancer too, so the two cancel out
choices.why: A function gets its capacity from the platform; nothing cancels, and that is why the pair costs more.

choices.text: Because one machine alone is not the same service
choices.why: Right: it has no second copy when it fails. A fair comparison prices the machines it takes to offer what the function offers.

choices.text: Because AWS sells t3.medium instances in pairs
choices.why: Instances are sold one at a time; the pair is a design choice from lesson 4.

choices.text: Because a t3.medium is too small to run Python
choices.why: Python runs on far smaller machines; size is not the argument here.

prompt: Two workloads each serve 20 million requests a month at the same size. A is steady all day; B arrives in a two-hour rush every evening. Which statement holds?
hint: A machine is sized for the busiest hour.

choices.text: Both cost the same on either, since the monthly totals are equal
choices.why: The function's total follows the total, but a machine is paid for the capacity of the peak.

choices.text: The machine costs less for B, since it idles twenty-two hours a day
choices.why: Idle hours are paid hours; the machine for B is the bigger one, and it idles at full price.

choices.text: The function costs the same for both; the machine for B has to be sized for the rush
choices.why: Right. Same requests, same function bill; the rush pushes B's machine up and B towards the function.

choices.text: The function costs more for B, because bursts are billed at a higher rate
choices.why: The rates per request and per GB-second are the same at any hour; the total follows the requests.

prompt: Reserved pricing lowers the machine's hourly price. What happens to the crossover with the function?
hint: The flat line moves down.

choices.text: It moves right, so the function wins at more volumes
choices.why: A cheaper machine is beaten by the function over a shorter stretch, not a longer one.

choices.text: It stays put, because reserving changes only when you pay
choices.why: Reserving changes the hourly price itself, and the crossover is that price divided by the function's.

choices.text: It disappears: a reserved machine is cheaper at every volume
choices.why: Below the crossover the function still costs less; at zero requests it costs nothing at all.

choices.text: It moves left: the machine starts winning at a lower volume
choices.why: Right. The sheet's 1-year t3.medium moves the first crossing from 25.3 to 15.9 million.

prompt: What does a Cloudflare Worker run in, where Lambda gives each environment a small virtual machine?
hint: It comes from the JavaScript engine in Chrome.

choices.text: A V8 isolate, in a process shared with other scripts
choices.why: Right. Isolates are far cheaper to create than virtual machines, which is why Workers start almost at once.

choices.text: A container started for each request that arrives
choices.why: No container is started per request; that start-up cost is exactly what isolates avoid.

choices.text: A dedicated virtual machine in a region you pick yourself
choices.why: There is no region to pick by default, and no machine of your own.

choices.text: The visitor's own browser, as a service worker
choices.why: A service worker runs in the browser; a Cloudflare Worker runs in Cloudflare's edge locations.

prompt: A Worker answering users in São Paulo makes three queries per request to a database in us-east-1. What did running the code at the edge buy?
hint: Where is the data?

choices.text: A faster response, since the Worker skips the cold start
choices.why: The start is quick, but three trips to Virginia per request are still paid on every call.

choices.text: Little: each request still crosses an ocean three times
choices.why: Right. The code moved to the user and the data stayed an ocean away.

choices.text: Lower load on the database, as the edge caches all queries
choices.why: A Worker caches nothing unless its code does; the database sees every query.

choices.text: Nothing, because Workers cannot reach databases
choices.why: They can reach one over the network; the problem is how far away it is.

prompt: A library needs Node's full file system API and a module compiled to native code. Where does it run with the least change?
hint: Which runtime is a full Node.js?

choices.text: In a Cloudflare Worker, since Workers run JavaScript
choices.why: Workers run JavaScript, but not all of Node, and native modules are out of reach.

choices.text: In the page's own JavaScript, in the browser
choices.why: A browser has no Node file system API and loads no native modules.

choices.text: In a Lambda function on a Node.js runtime
choices.why: Right. It is a full Node.js with a disk at `/tmp`; the native module has to be built for Lambda's platform.

choices.text: In edge code on Vercel, which runs before the cache
choices.why: Edge code runs in a restricted runtime of the same family as Workers, with the same limits.

prompt: Cloudflare bills a Worker for requests and for ___ time, not for the time it spends waiting on another service.
hint: The processor.

prompt: Put a change on Vercel or Netlify in order, from code to live site.
hint: The preview comes before the merge.
items: Push a branch and open a pull request
A reviewer opens the preview URL
The pull request is merged into main
The build of main becomes the live site
trap: The preview URL cannot come before the build: it is the build, at an address of its own.

prompt: Which project fits Vercel or Netlify worst?
hint: Where does the product's weight sit?

choices.text: A documentation site built by a static site generator from Markdown
choices.why: A fit: every push rebuilds it, and it is served from a CDN.

choices.text: A marketing site whose only API is a contact form
choices.why: A fit: the form is one function in `api/` beside the pages.

choices.text: The front end of an app whose API runs elsewhere
choices.why: A fit: the platform builds and serves the front end, which calls the API over HTTP.

choices.text: A video service whose back end transcodes each upload for an hour
choices.why: Right. The back end is most of the product and runs far past a function's limits.

prompt: Why do teams adopt Vercel or Netlify, according to the lesson?
hint: One step of the workflow.

choices.text: A preview URL for every pull request
choices.why: Right. A change is reviewed as a page, by whoever needs to see it.

choices.text: The longest function durations of any platform
choices.why: Their functions carry the same kind of limits as Lambda's; duration is not the draw.

choices.text: A virtual machine for each site, with SSH access
choices.why: There is no machine to log in to; that is the point of the model.

choices.text: Hosting a relational database beside the site
choices.why: Heavy database work is one of the things the lesson places elsewhere.

prompt: Which of these fit inside a single Lambda call? Choose all that apply.
hint: 15 minutes, and 6 MB each way for a synchronous call.

choices.text: A 25-minute batch job
choices.why: Past the 15-minute maximum; it has to be cut into steps or run elsewhere.

choices.text: A report that takes 10 minutes to build
choices.why: Right. Under 15 minutes, provided the timeout is raised from its default.

choices.text: A 4 MB JSON response to a synchronous request
choices.why: Right. Under the 6 MB cap on a synchronous response.

choices.text: A 50 MB file returned in the response body
choices.why: Past the 6 MB cap; the function puts the file in object storage and returns a link.

prompt: A burst creates 800 environments of a function, and its PostgreSQL database starts refusing connections. Which change would NOT help?
hint: The problem is how many connections are open at once.

choices.text: A connection proxy such as RDS Proxy
choices.why: It helps: a small pool of real connections is lent to all the environments.

choices.text: Giving the function more memory
choices.why: Right, it does not help. Each copy gets faster, but just as many copies each open a connection.

choices.text: A reserved concurrency limit on the function
choices.why: It helps: fewer copies at once means fewer connections, at the price of turning some requests away.

choices.text: Moving the data to a database reached over HTTP
choices.why: It helps: with no long-lived connections there is no pool to run out of.

prompt: Match each wall of a Lambda function to what a design does about it.
hint: Each answer moves the work or the data somewhere else.

pairs.right: Return a link to object storage
Keep the session in a database
Put a connection proxy in front of the database

prompt: Which of these jobs is the worst fit for a function?
hint: Bursts, quick, remembers nothing.

choices.text: Resizing a photo when it is uploaded
choices.why: A good fit: an event, a short job, nobody waiting.

choices.text: An internal API called a few hundred times a day
choices.why: A good fit: quiet most of the day, so it costs almost nothing between calls.

choices.text: A game server holding a room's state for hours
choices.why: Right. Its value is what the process remembers, and a function is built to forget.

choices.text: Sending a report every Monday morning
choices.why: A good fit: a schedule trigger, and the job ends in minutes at most.

prompt: A team plans to move its Lambda functions to Cloudflare Workers one day. What can they keep portable now?
hint: The lesson separates the logic from the wiring.

choices.text: The handler's signature, `(event, context)`
choices.why: Lambda's `(event, context)` and Workers' `fetch(request)` differ; the signature is wiring.

choices.text: The event shapes the functions read from triggers
choices.why: Event shapes belong to the vendor's triggers, and they change with the platform.

choices.text: The IAM roles the functions run with
choices.why: IAM is AWS's; permissions are rewritten on any other platform.

choices.text: The business logic, kept apart from the handler
choices.why: Right. Logic that takes plain values and returns plain values moves; only the edges are rewritten.

prompt: Match each platform to how it runs your code.
hint: Region, edge, git or hour.

pairs.right: A small virtual machine per environment, in a region you choose
V8 isolates in edge locations close to the user
A site built from every git push, with functions alongside
One machine you run, paid for by the hour

right_distractors: A copy of the code in every visitor's browser

prompt: Order these from the most left to you to the least, on lesson 1's line.
hint: Functions sit between PaaS and SaaS.
trap: PaaS after functions is the usual slip: with PaaS you still decide how many instances run.

prompt: A photo site: a few hundred uploads a day each need a thumbnail, and the public gallery page serves 60 requests a second, all day. Which split fits this lesson?
hint: Treat the two workloads separately.

choices.text: Thumbnails on functions, the gallery on machines
choices.why: Right. The uploads are spiky events; the gallery is steady load far past the crossover.

choices.text: Functions for both, since both are web traffic
choices.why: The gallery's 60 a second, all day, is steady load, where the machine line is lower.

choices.text: Machines for both, to be rid of cold starts
choices.why: A few hundred thumbnails a day would keep a machine idle almost all the time.

choices.text: Machines for the thumbnails, functions for the gallery
choices.why: The reverse of the shape: the bursty work gets the machine and the steady work the function.

prompt: A Lambda function is quiet all night and gets a burst every morning at nine. Users complain that the first minutes are slow. Which change targets exactly that?
hint: The slowness is the environments being created.

choices.text: Moving the database client inside the handler
choices.why: That makes every call slower, warm or cold.

choices.text: Provisioned concurrency before nine
choices.why: Right. Environments are ready before the burst arrives; a lighter init helps any that still have to be created.

choices.text: A longer timeout on the function
choices.why: The calls are slow, not cut off; the timeout does not touch start-up.

choices.text: A dead-letter queue for the failed requests
choices.why: Nothing failed, and HTTP calls have a caller waiting, not a queue.
